item.statement: In about 1 in 5 deaths blamed on mephedrone, tests after death found none of the drug.
item.why: By October 2011, 128 deaths in the UK and nearby islands had been linked to mephedrone, and in 25 of them tests found none. A negative test may miss earlier use, and a positive one does not prove the drug caused the death.

lines.short: In 25 of 128 alleged deaths, tests after death found no mephedrone.
lines.but: A positive test does not prove cause. A negative test may miss earlier use.
how: By October 2011, 128 deaths in the UK and nearby islands had been linked to mephedrone; 13 results were still pending.
Of 62 deaths studied, mephedrone was the only substance found in 8. Other drugs were common.
One person died weeks later in hospital and had none found after death. Their earlier test evidence is not given.
The authors say tests and incomplete reporting may also miss deaths. They cannot give a death rate.

item.statement: A negative fentanyl test strip means no other unexpected drugs are in the mix either.
item.why: A strip only shows whether fentanyl is there, not other drugs in the mix or how much. At one drug-checking service, 24 of 159 lab-checked samples held a newer benzo that none of the people who brought them expected.

lines.short: A test for one drug did not show other drugs in the mix, or how much.
lines.but: Only two small studies tested this directly. The rest is how the tests are made.
how: In one lab study, MDMA samples with caffeine or amphetamine mixed in looked the same on a colour test.
At one drug-checking service, 24 of 159 samples checked by a lab had a newer benzodiazepine. None of the people who brought them expected it. Most also had fentanyl.
Fentanyl strips only show if fentanyl is there. They do not show how much.
No study tested whether a negative result makes a drug less risky.

item.statement: Pills don't help people stay away from heavy drinking.
item.why: One tablet, naltrexone, does a little: in dozens of trials about 46 in 100 people on it went back to heavy drinking, against 54 in 100 on dummy pills. It helped less, if at all, with stopping completely, and most people in the trials also had counselling.

lines.short: On naltrexone, 46 in 100 went back to heavy drinking, against 54 on dummy pills.
lines.but: Most people in the trials were middle-aged men who had already stopped drinking and had counselling.
how: Naltrexone is a tablet. Dozens of trials gave it or dummy pills, mostly for 3 months, usually with counselling as well.
About 46 in 100 on naltrexone went back to heavy drinking, against 54 in 100 on dummy pills. It helped less, if at all, with stopping completely.
People on naltrexone drank on about 5 fewer days in every 100. Feeling sick, dizziness and vomiting were more common.
When compared directly, naltrexone and acamprosate did about the same, but most people in that comparison were in one trial.

item.statement: People who meet a 'being' on DMT mostly describe it as hostile.
item.why: Most said the being seemed conscious, intelligent and kind, though 41 in 100 felt fear at some point. Only people who'd had such a meeting were asked, so this can't show how often it happens.

lines.short: Mostly a being, a guide, a spirit or an alien. 69 in 100 said it gave them a message. People who said they'd met God without drugs told similar stories.
lines.but: Only people who'd had such a meeting took part, so we can't tell how often it happens.
how: In 2018, 2,561 adults described their most memorable meeting with a being after smoking or vaping DMT. Looking back, 65 in 100 judged it more real than everyday life.
On DMT, most said the being seemed conscious, intelligent and kind. Still, 41 in 100 felt fear at some point.
It's not just DMT. Of 809 people who said they met God or a higher power without drugs, 86 in 100 called it kind. 78 in 100 said they got a message.
28 in 100 recalled being atheists before the meeting, and 10 in 100 said they were now. Without drugs, the share fell too. But people recalled their old beliefs years later.

item.statement: Most people who met a 'being' on DMT later judged the meeting more real than everyday life.
item.why: Looking back, 65 in 100 of 2,561 adults said so, and 69 in 100 said the being gave them a message. People who said they'd met God without drugs told similar stories.

lines.short: Mostly a being, a guide, a spirit or an alien. 69 in 100 said it gave them a message. People who said they'd met God without drugs told similar stories.
lines.but: Only people who'd had such a meeting took part, so we can't tell how often it happens.

On DMT, most said the being seemed conscious, intelligent and kind. Still, 41 in 100 felt fear at some point.
It's not just DMT. Of 809 people who said they met God or a higher power without drugs, 86 in 100 called it kind. 78 in 100 said they got a message.
28 in 100 recalled being atheists before the meeting, and 10 in 100 said they were now. Without drugs, the share fell too. But people recalled their old beliefs years later.

item.statement: Towns that trained more people to give naloxone, the overdose rescue medicine, had lower opioid death rates.
item.why: In Massachusetts, opioid death rates were about a fifth lower where more than 1 in 1,000 people were trained and given naloxone. It's a link, not proof: the study mostly compared later years with earlier ones.

lines.short: Naloxone kits are linked to fewer deaths from heroin and other opioids, but it's not proven. At least 96 in 100 people given naloxone by someone trained survived.
lines.but: Surviving doesn't prove naloxone saved a life, since most overdoses aren't fatal, and only one study compared death rates.
how: In 19 Massachusetts towns, 2006 to 2009, 2,912 people who might see an opioid overdose got training and nasal naloxone. They reported 327 rescue attempts.
Where more than 1 in 1,000 people were trained, opioid death rates were about a fifth lower, and nearly half lower after allowing for other differences.
Every town had the programme by 2008, so the study mostly compared later years with earlier ones. It never printed how many people died.
Across 17 studies, trained people gave naloxone 2,336 times, mostly for heroin overdoses; 20 are known to have died. Since most overdoses aren't fatal, lives saved are unknown.

item.statement: The old scare that LSD breaks your chromosomes turned out to be right.
item.why: The 1967 scare began with LSD added to blood cells in a lab dish. When 32 patients were tested before and after pure LSD there was no clear rise in damaged cells, though these were small studies of blood cells only.

lines.short: Studies from 1967 to 1970 found no clear rise in broken chromosomes after pure LSD. Early reports of more breaks came mostly from people using many drugs.
lines.but: Small studies that only looked at blood cells under a microscope; the best had no group without LSD.
how: The 1967 scare began with LSD added to blood cells from two people in a lab dish, plus one patient with no 'before' test.
Two 1967 studies found more breaks in people who had taken LSD, with no 'before' test. In one, patients on other drugs but no LSD had about as many breaks.
The best study tested 32 patients before and after pure LSD. Damaged cells went from about 4 in 100 to 6, maybe by chance.
All these studies looked at blood cells under a microscope, not sperm or eggs. A 1971 review linked raised breaks mainly to street LSD and many other drugs.

item.statement: In a US test, about 1 in 5 CBD products bought online also contained THC.
item.why: Of 84 CBD oils, tinctures and vape liquids bought online in 2016, about 1 in 5 also held THC. No one took them, so the test can't say whether they cause a high or a positive drug test.

lines.short: Mostly not. Of 84 CBD products bought online in the US in 2016, only about 3 in 10 matched their CBD label. About 1 in 5 also held THC.
lines.but: One test of products bought online in 2016; products sold in shops, or today, may differ.
how: CBD is a substance from the cannabis plant. Researchers bought every CBD oil, tincture and vape liquid with a CBD label they found online.
A lab that did not know the labels tested them. 36 held more CBD than the label said, and 22 held less.
Vape liquids were most often wrong: 21 of 24 were off by more than a tenth, mostly holding more CBD than labelled.
No one took the products, and no urine was tested. So this can't say if they cause a high or a positive drug test.

item.statement: In lab tests, believing a drink was alcoholic made people drink more of it, whatever was really in the glass.
item.why: Men told their drink had vodka drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, whether or not it did; real vodka made no clear difference. These were lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s, with low blood alcohol.

lines.short: In lab tests, partly: believing they drank alcohol made men drink more.
lines.but: Lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s; the drinking test lasted 15 minutes, with low blood alcohol.
how: 64 men were told at random that their drink had vodka or not, and were given vodka or not, also at random. Half had a history of drinking problems.
Men told it had vodka drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, whatever was really in the glass. Real vodka made no clear difference to how much they drank.
Across 36 similar experiments, believing you had drunk alcohol went with more drinking, but not with changes in mood or memory. Sexual arousal rose on average, but that varied a lot between studies.
The alcohol itself, not the belief, affected memory, coordination, body sensations and mood. Blood alcohol in the drinking study stayed low, so heavier drinking may differ.

item.statement: In lab experiments, sexual arousal rose on average when people believed they'd drunk alcohol.
item.why: Across 36 experiments, believing you had drunk alcohol went with more sexual arousal on average, though that varied a lot between studies. Mood and memory were changed by the alcohol itself, not the belief.

lines.short: In lab tests, partly: believing they drank alcohol made men drink more.
lines.but: Lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s; the drinking test lasted 15 minutes, with low blood alcohol.
how: 64 men were told at random that their drink had vodka or not, and were given vodka or not, also at random. Half had a history of drinking problems.
Men told it had vodka drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, whatever was really in the glass. Real vodka made no clear difference to how much they drank.
Across 36 similar experiments, believing you had drunk alcohol went with more drinking, but not with changes in mood or memory. Sexual arousal rose on average, but that varied a lot between studies.
The alcohol itself, not the belief, affected memory, coordination, body sensations and mood. Blood alcohol in the drinking study stayed low, so heavier drinking may differ.

item.statement: Doctors have reported people having trouble walking after using laughing gas.
item.why: In doctors' reports on 100 people with health problems after nitrous oxide, 58 had trouble walking and 80 had numbness or tingling. Of the 100, 57 had used it for fun and 25 had it in surgery.

lines.short: Yes: doctors have described nerve damage after nitrous oxide (laughing gas). In an online survey, about 4 in 100 people who used it in the past year reported lasting numbness.
lines.but: No doctor checked these answers and people chose to take part, so it can't show how common lasting numbness is after nitrous oxide.
how: A review pooled doctors' reports on 100 people with health problems after nitrous oxide (laughing gas): 57 had used it for fun, 25 in surgery.
80 had numbness or tingling and 58 had trouble walking. Of 75 who had a spine scan, 51 showed a change in the spinal cord.
58 of 82 tested had low vitamin B12. But the search only found reports mentioning B12, so this is partly built in.
In an online survey, 200 of 4,633 people who used nitrous oxide in the past year reported numbness or tingling lasting days or weeks.

item.statement: Ecstasy isn't a drug people become dependent on.
item.why: Some do: in US surveys, about 4 in 100 people who had used it recently met the criteria for dependence, and more in some small groups. The checklists were made for other drugs, so the numbers can't be applied to everyone who uses ecstasy.

lines.short: Yes, some do. How many depends on who's asked: about 4 in 100 people who'd used it recently in US surveys, but up to 73 in 100 in small groups.
lines.but: Every checklist was made for other drugs, and most studies used volunteers, so the numbers can't be applied to everyone who uses ecstasy.
how: In two US surveys of the general public, about 4 in 100 people who had used ecstasy recently met the criteria for dependence. Among clubgoers, young people in detention and volunteers, it was 16 to 22 in 100.
Three small samples gave much higher numbers: 43 to 73 in 100 met the criteria at some point in their lives. They included people in drug treatment and people who had taken at least 250 pills.
The one study that followed people found that 93 in 100 of those dependent at the start no longer were after about three years. That group was small: about 12 to 14 people, by our count.

The symptoms reported most included carrying on despite problems, lots of time using or recovering, tolerance and withdrawal. Pills sold as ecstasy may hold methamphetamine, so some of this may be dependence on another drug.

item.statement: Light weed smoking wears down lung function over the years, the way tobacco does.
item.why: In a 20-year study of about 5,000 adults, light cannabis smoking did not lower lung function; tobacco did. Smoking cannabis is still linked to cough, phlegm and wheeze, and too few people smoked it heavily for years to know what that does.

lines.short: Smoking cannabis is linked to cough, phlegm and wheeze; light smoking didn't lower lung function.
lines.but: Many people also smoked tobacco, so the studies can't say how much comes from cannabis.
how: In two long-running studies, breathing symptoms eased in people who stopped.
In a 20-year study of about 5,000 adults, light cannabis smoking did not lower lung function; tobacco did.
Too few people smoked cannabis heavily for years to know what that does.
In one study, symptoms eased after a month of using a vaporizer instead of smoking, but it had no comparison group.

item.statement: The cough and wheeze linked to smoking weed tend to ease when people stop.
item.why: In two long-running studies, breathing symptoms eased in people who stopped. Many people also smoked tobacco, so the studies can't say how much of it comes from cannabis.

lines.short: Smoking cannabis is linked to cough, phlegm and wheeze; light smoking didn't lower lung function.
lines.but: Many people also smoked tobacco, so the studies can't say how much comes from cannabis.
how: In two long-running studies, breathing symptoms eased in people who stopped.
In a 20-year study of about 5,000 adults, light cannabis smoking did not lower lung function; tobacco did.
Too few people smoked cannabis heavily for years to know what that does.
In one study, symptoms eased after a month of using a vaporizer instead of smoking, but it had no comparison group.

item.statement: Weed edibles are too mild to put a small child in hospital.
item.why: Of young children in US poison-centre calls about edibles, more than 1 in 5 were admitted to hospital and 35 needed a breathing tube; no deaths were reported. Such calls rose about 15 times over from 2017 to 2021.

lines.short: Calls to US poison centres about young children eating edibles rose about 15 times over, 2017 to 2021.
lines.but: These are only the calls that were made, and the study can't say why the number rose.
how: Most of the children were 1 to 4 years old and ate the edible at home.
More than 1 in 5 were admitted to hospital, and 35 needed a breathing tube. No deaths were reported.
The authors suggest changes in the law, the pandemic or more calling, but the data can't separate these.

item.statement: Some people who use weed regularly get bouts of severe vomiting.
item.why: In published cases, the bouts ended when people stopped cannabis: 62 of 64 who stopped got completely better, while the 21 who kept using did not. Nobody knows how common it is.

lines.short: Bouts of severe vomiting with regular cannabis use; in reported cases, stopping ended them.
lines.but: Published cases only: nobody knows how common it is, and fewer than half were followed up.
how: A 2017 review pooled 211 published cases; all had bouts of vomiting with severe nausea, and most had belly pain.
About 3 in 4 used cannabis daily or more, but a quarter had used it for a year or less before it started.
Most found that hot baths or showers eased it for a while, but many people with other kinds of repeated vomiting use hot showers too.
Of 64 people whose stopping was recorded, 62 got completely better; the 21 who kept using did not.

item.statement: Most people with weed-linked vomiting bouts found hot baths or showers eased them for a while.
item.why: That is from 211 published cases, though many people with other kinds of repeated vomiting use hot showers too. What ended the bouts, in the cases followed up, was stopping cannabis.

lines.short: Bouts of severe vomiting with regular cannabis use; in reported cases, stopping ended them.
lines.but: Published cases only: nobody knows how common it is, and fewer than half were followed up.
how: A 2017 review pooled 211 published cases; all had bouts of vomiting with severe nausea, and most had belly pain.
About 3 in 4 used cannabis daily or more, but a quarter had used it for a year or less before it started.
Most found that hot baths or showers eased it for a while, but many people with other kinds of repeated vomiting use hot showers too.
Of 64 people whose stopping was recorded, 62 got completely better; the 21 who kept using did not.

item.statement: Nicotine patches and gum don't actually help people quit smoking.
item.why: They help, modestly: after 6 months or more, about 16 in 100 had stopped with nicotine replacement, against 10 or 11 in 100 without. Many of the trials were paid for by drug companies.

lines.short: Nicotine patches, gum and similar help people who want to stop smoking.
lines.but: The gain is modest, and many trials were paid for by drug companies.
how: After 6 months or more, about 16 in 100 had stopped with nicotine replacement, against about 10 or 11 in 100 without.
The gain was bigger with a lot of support (about 8 more in 100) than with little (about 2 more).
Each form, from patches to sprays, did better than its own comparison.
These were people trying to stop, so the trials say nothing about anyone else.

item.statement: When UK experts ranked 20 drugs by overall harm, heroin came out as the most harmful.
item.why: Alcohol came top, mostly for the harm it does to other people; for the person using, crack, heroin and meth scored worst. The scores are one panel's views, and alcohol's top score partly reflects how many people drink.

lines.short: Experts have tried: a UK panel ranked alcohol most harmful overall, mostly for harm to other people. For the person using, crack, heroin and meth scored worst.
lines.but: The scores are one panel's views, not measures, and alcohol's top score partly reflects how many people drink.
how: In 2010, experts scored 20 drugs on 16 harms in one day. A 2007 expert ranking put legal alcohol and tobacco above LSD and ecstasy.
Alcohol scored 72 of 100, 46 of them for harm to others. Critics say one score mixes harm per person with how many people use.
Tobacco scored zero for deaths like overdose. Lung cancer was counted elsewhere. The authors agreed it probably kills more than the other 19 drugs combined.
In an online survey, 1,501 people rated drug harms much like experts did. Of the 603 allowed to rate heroin, 467 had never used it.

item.statement: Tobacco probably kills more people than the 19 other drugs UK experts ranked, heroin and alcohol included, put together.
item.why: The ranking's own authors agreed it probably does. Yet tobacco scored zero for deaths like overdose, because lung cancer was counted elsewhere in the scores.

lines.short: Experts have tried: a UK panel ranked alcohol most harmful overall, mostly for harm to other people. For the person using, crack, heroin and meth scored worst.
lines.but: The scores are one panel's views, not measures, and alcohol's top score partly reflects how many people drink.
how: In 2010, experts scored 20 drugs on 16 harms in one day. A 2007 expert ranking put legal alcohol and tobacco above LSD and ecstasy.
Alcohol scored 72 of 100, 46 of them for harm to others. Critics say one score mixes harm per person with how many people use.
Tobacco scored zero for deaths like overdose. Lung cancer was counted elsewhere. The authors agreed it probably kills more than the other 19 drugs combined.
In an online survey, 1,501 people rated drug harms much like experts did. Of the 603 allowed to rate heroin, 467 had never used it.

item.statement: In the famous 'Rat Park' experiments, rats living together left the morphine water alone.
item.why: They drank less of it than rats kept alone, but only in some tests; in one, they drank more. Two later attempts to repeat a Rat Park study did not find the same result, and rats aren't people.

lines.short: Less than is often said. Rats living together drank less morphine water, but only in some tests.
lines.but: All of this was in rats, so it says nothing direct about people.
how: In 1979, by the last test, rats kept alone drank 5 to over 16 times as much sweet morphine water as rats living together.
In 1978, when morphine water was almost all they had to drink, the rats living together drank more of it.
In all three studies, the two groups drank morphine water from different machines, measured differently. That could explain part of the gap.
Two later experiments meant to repeat the 1981 Rat Park morphine study did not find the same result.

item.statement: In one study, people who had quit heavy weed use still scored worse on thinking tests a year later.
item.why: People who had stopped heavy use for a year or more scored no differently on any test from people who had not used. Studies of people 3 to 8 weeks after stopping disagree, and researchers read the evidence in opposite ways.

lines.short: Not clear. Where studies asked people to stop for over 3 days, the gap was small.
lines.but: This compared different studies, not the same people before and after they stopped.
how: A review of 69 studies found a smaller gap in studies that asked people to stop for more than 3 days. The gap might be zero, but one almost as big as the overall gap is not ruled out.
Studies of people who had stopped for about 3 to 8 weeks disagree. Some found lower scores on some tests; others found none.
Few studies followed people for longer. In one, people who had stopped heavy use for a year or more did not score differently on any test from people who had not used.
Two reviews read this evidence in opposite ways. Researchers disagree.

item.statement: Alcohol withdrawal is unpleasant, but it doesn't cause seizures.
item.why: It can: in old trials, about 8 in 100 people going through alcohol withdrawal on dummy pills had a seizure. With calming medicines called benzodiazepines, about 1 in 100 did.

lines.short: In old trials, benzodiazepines cut seizures: about 1 in 100, against 8 on dummy pills.
lines.but: The trials were from the 1960s to 1983, and few people had seizures.
how: Benzodiazepines are calming medicines. Old trials gave them or dummy pills to people going through alcohol withdrawal.
About 1 in 100 people on a benzodiazepine had a seizure, against about 8 in 100 on dummy pills. Delirium was also less common: about 2 in 100 against 6.
Other medicines were not clearly better or worse. One kind of antipsychotic given on its own was followed by more seizures and delirium than benzodiazepines.
Few trials looked at people who already had the DTs.

item.statement: On some brain scans, parts of the brain looked larger, not smaller, in people who used meth.
item.why: Studies disagree: soon after stopping, some brain areas looked smaller, while other studies found some larger. The groups also differed in smoking, schooling and low mood, and some differences may not last.

lines.short: Some brain areas looked smaller soon after stopping. Other studies found some larger.
lines.but: Smoking, schooling and low mood also differ, and some differences may not last.
how: Soon after stopping, some brain areas had less grey matter (up to about 11% in one study).
Other studies, after 3 to 4 months off meth or during use, found some areas larger.
Smoking, less schooling and low mood also differed between the groups.
In one study, grey matter grew in several areas over the first month without meth, but only by a lenient test.

item.statement: The link between weed and car crashes gets much smaller once drivers' drinking is taken into account.
item.why: Studies that allowed for alcohol found drivers with cannabis in a test had 1.1 to 1.2 times the odds of a crash; studies that did not found 1.7 to 1.8 times. Either way, cannabis in a test was linked to more crashes.

lines.short: Drivers with cannabis in a test were linked to more crashes.
lines.but: These studies compare crashed drivers with others, so they cannot show one driver's chance of crashing.
how: Across 28 results from 21 studies in 13 countries, drivers with cannabis found in a test had about 1.2 to 1.4 times the odds of a crash, or of being at fault in one.
An older review found 1.9 times. Re-checking its counts and allowing for other factors brought the same studies to between 1.2 and 1.4.
Studies that allowed for alcohol found 1.1 to 1.2 times. Studies that did not found 1.7 to 1.8 times.
A positive test shows cannabis was in the body, not that a driver was impaired.

item.statement: Caffeine can keep people awake longer in the night without them noticing.
item.why: Across 24 studies, caffeine made time awake in the night longer and sleep lighter. Yet in five studies, people did not report more time awake in the night.

lines.short: After caffeine, people slept about 45 minutes less than on nights without caffeine.
lines.but: The people studied were healthy adults with low to moderate usual caffeine intake, so heavy users, teenagers and older adults may differ.
how: 24 studies compared nights after caffeine with nights without it, in the same people.
Caffeine made falling asleep slower, time awake in the night longer, and sleep lighter.
The more caffeine, and the closer to bedtime, the more sleep people lost.
In five studies, people did not report more time awake in the night.

item.statement: Since weed usually comes first, it must be what leads people on to other illegal drugs.
item.why: Coming first doesn't prove it leads on: a computer model in which cannabis did nothing still produced the same pattern. Whether cannabis plays any part is still not known, and experts disagree.

lines.short: Not known. Cannabis usually comes first, but that does not prove it leads on.
lines.but: Shared risks and access to other drugs could still explain the cannabis link.
how: In New Zealand, at least 86 in 100 young people who used other illegal drugs had used cannabis a year or more before.
Australian twins grew up together. The one starting cannabis before 17 more often used cocaine or other stimulants: 48 in 100 against 26 in 100.
A computer model where cannabis did nothing still made the same pattern. Some people were likelier to use any drug, and were offered cannabis first.
Experts disagreed about the New Zealand cannabis link. One said hidden factors no longer explain it away; another said factors changing with age still could.

item.statement: In published cases of people who kept vomiting while using cannabis regularly, most found hot baths or showers helped for a while.
item.why: Most of the 211 people in published cases found this. But many people with other kinds of repeated vomiting use hot showers too.

lines.short: Bouts of severe vomiting with regular cannabis use; in reported cases, stopping ended them.
lines.but: Published cases only: nobody knows how common it is, and fewer than half were followed up.
how: A 2017 review pooled 211 published cases; all had bouts of vomiting with severe nausea, and most had belly pain.
About 3 in 4 used cannabis daily or more, but a quarter had used it for a year or less before it started.
Most found that hot baths or showers eased it for a while, but many people with other kinds of repeated vomiting use hot showers too.
Of 64 people whose stopping was recorded, 62 got completely better; the 21 who kept using did not.

item.statement: Regular cannabis use can come with repeated vomiting. In published cases, most found hot showers or baths eased it for a while.
item.why: Most of the 211 people in published cases found this. But many people with other kinds of repeated vomiting use hot showers too.

lines.short: Bouts of severe vomiting with regular cannabis use; in reported cases, stopping ended them.
lines.but: Published cases only: nobody knows how common it is, and fewer than half were followed up.
how: A 2017 review pooled 211 published cases; all had bouts of vomiting with severe nausea, and most had belly pain.
About 3 in 4 used cannabis daily or more, but a quarter had used it for a year or less before it started.
Most found that hot baths or showers eased it for a while, but many people with other kinds of repeated vomiting use hot showers too.
Of 64 people whose stopping was recorded, 62 got completely better; the 21 who kept using did not.

item.statement: In death records from 27 US states, kratom was usually the only drug found when it was named a cause of death.
item.why: Only 7 of 91 had kratom alone; other drugs turned up in the rest, and fentanyl was named as a cause in 51.

lines.short: Kratom turned up in about 6 of every 1,000 overdose deaths in 27 US states in 2016–17. It was almost always found with other drugs.
lines.but: Testing for kratom varied and was not recorded, so some deaths with kratom were probably missed.
how: A CDC system gathered 27,338 overdose deaths from 27 US states, July 2016 to December 2017. Kratom was found in 152.
Kratom was named as a cause in 91 deaths. Other drugs turned up in 84 of them; fentanyl was named as a cause in 51.
Only 7 deaths had kratom as the only drug found. Even then, the report says other drugs cannot be ruled out.
The system counts mostly deaths where opioids played a part. With no count of people who use kratom, there is no death rate.

item.statement: When doctors wrote up people with health problems after laughing gas, most had numbness or tingling.
item.why: Of 100 people in published reports, 80 had numbness or tingling and 58 had trouble walking. Not all used it for fun: 25 had been given it in surgery.

lines.short: Yes: doctors have described nerve damage after nitrous oxide (laughing gas). In an online survey, about 4 in 100 people who used it in the past year reported lasting numbness.
lines.but: No doctor checked these answers and people chose to take part, so it can't show how common lasting numbness is after nitrous oxide.
how: A review pooled doctors' reports on 100 people with health problems after nitrous oxide (laughing gas): 57 had used it for fun, 25 in surgery.
80 had numbness or tingling and 58 had trouble walking. Of 75 who had a spine scan, 51 showed a change in the spinal cord.
58 of 82 tested had low vitamin B12. But the search only found reports mentioning B12, so this is partly built in.
In an online survey, 200 of 4,633 people who used nitrous oxide in the past year reported numbness or tingling lasting days or weeks.

item.statement: In safety reports about ecstasy, death was more common when the report also named an antidepressant.
item.why: In US reports, those cases had about 1.6 times the odds of a fatal outcome, and reports naming muscle relaxants or anesthetics had higher odds still. These are voluntary reports, so they can't show cause, and nobody knows how many people took each mix.

lines.short: In safety reports, ecstasy cases that also named an antidepressant ended in death more often.
lines.but: Voluntary reports cannot show cause, and nobody knows how many people took each mix.
how: In 946 US reports about ecstasy, those that also named an antidepressant had about 1.6 times the odds of a fatal outcome.
Reports naming other kinds of medicine had higher odds still: about 8 times for muscle relaxants and about 7 times for anesthetics.
In a survey of 216 adults, 76 in 100 who mixed ecstasy with an antidepressant still felt euphoria. They also reported more sweating, headache, dizziness and muscle stiffness.
The review's authors suggest, without data, that people whose effects were muted may have taken more.

item.statement: In studies of twins, the twin who used cannabis as a teen, mostly lightly, lost clearly more IQ than the other twin.
item.why: No clear extra loss, though these studies could miss a small one. One study found about 6 points lost after years of dependence.

lines.short: Not shown either way. In one study, people dependent for years lost about 6 IQ points.
lines.but: Other differences between people could explain it. Twin studies of lighter use found no clear extra loss.
how: In New Zealand, 874 people took IQ tests as children and again at 38.
The 38 people who were dependent on cannabis at 3 or more of 5 check-ups lost about 6 points from their childhood scores. People who never used gained a little.
Another researcher showed that differences in family background could produce a similar pattern. The first team found that family background did not change their result.
In US and British twin studies, mostly of lighter teenage use, the twin who used did not lose clearly more than the twin who did not. These studies could miss a small loss.

item.statement: After meeting a 'being' on DMT, fewer people call themselves atheists. The same happens after drug-free 'God' encounters.
item.why: Among people who'd had such meetings, 28 in 100 recalled being atheists before a DMT encounter and 10 in 100 said they were now, and the share fell without drugs too. But they were recalling old beliefs years later.

lines.short: Mostly a being, a guide, a spirit or an alien. 69 in 100 said it gave them a message. People who said they'd met God without drugs told similar stories.
lines.but: Only people who'd had such a meeting took part, so we can't tell how often it happens.
how: In 2018, 2,561 adults described their most memorable meeting with a being after smoking or vaping DMT. Looking back, 65 in 100 judged it more real than everyday life.
On DMT, most said the being seemed conscious, intelligent and kind. Still, 41 in 100 felt fear at some point.
It's not just DMT. Of 809 people who said they met God or a higher power without drugs, 86 in 100 called it kind. 78 in 100 said they got a message.
28 in 100 recalled being atheists before the meeting, and 10 in 100 said they were now. Without drugs, the share fell too. But people recalled their old beliefs years later.

item.statement: In lab tests, men who were told their drink had vodka in it drank more, whatever was really in the glass.
item.why: They drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, while real vodka made no clear difference to how much they drank. These were lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s, with low blood alcohol.

lines.short: In lab tests, partly: believing they drank alcohol made men drink more.
lines.but: Lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s; the drinking test lasted 15 minutes, with low blood alcohol.
how: 64 men were told at random that their drink had vodka or not, and were given vodka or not, also at random. Half had a history of drinking problems.
Men told it had vodka drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, whatever was really in the glass. Real vodka made no clear difference to how much they drank.
Across 36 similar experiments, believing you had drunk alcohol went with more drinking, but not with changes in mood or memory. Sexual arousal rose on average, but that varied a lot between studies.
The alcohol itself, not the belief, affected memory, coordination, body sensations and mood. Blood alcohol in the drinking study stayed low, so heavier drinking may differ.

item.statement: Regular cannabis use can come with bouts of severe vomiting. In most reported cases, it ended when people stopped using.
item.why: Of 64 people whose stopping was recorded, 62 got completely better. Nobody knows how common it is.

lines.short: Bouts of severe vomiting with regular cannabis use; in reported cases, stopping ended them.
lines.but: Published cases only: nobody knows how common it is, and fewer than half were followed up.
how: A 2017 review pooled 211 published cases; all had bouts of vomiting with severe nausea, and most had belly pain.
About 3 in 4 used cannabis daily or more, but a quarter had used it for a year or less before it started.
Most found that hot baths or showers eased it for a while, but many people with other kinds of repeated vomiting use hot showers too.
Of 64 people whose stopping was recorded, 62 got completely better; the 21 who kept using did not.

item.statement: In one study, people a year or more off heavy cannabis use did as well on tests as people who hadn't used.
item.why: They scored no differently on any test, and a big review found smaller gaps in studies that asked people to stop for over 3 days. But few studies have followed people that long, and researchers disagree.

lines.short: Not clear. Where studies asked people to stop for over 3 days, the gap was small.
lines.but: This compared different studies, not the same people before and after they stopped.
how: A review of 69 studies found a smaller gap in studies that asked people to stop for more than 3 days. The gap might be zero, but one almost as big as the overall gap is not ruled out.
Studies of people who had stopped for about 3 to 8 weeks disagree. Some found lower scores on some tests; others found none.
Few studies followed people for longer. In one, people who had stopped heavy use for a year or more did not score differently on any test from people who had not used.
Two reviews read this evidence in opposite ways. Researchers disagree.

item.statement: Caffeine kept people awake longer in the night, yet in five studies people did not say they had been awake more.
item.why: Across 24 studies, caffeine made falling asleep slower and time awake longer; in five, people did not report more time awake.

lines.short: After caffeine, people slept about 45 minutes less than on nights without caffeine.
lines.but: The people studied were healthy adults with low to moderate usual caffeine intake, so heavy users, teenagers and older adults may differ.
how: 24 studies compared nights after caffeine with nights without it, in the same people.
Caffeine made falling asleep slower, time awake in the night longer, and sleep lighter.
The more caffeine, and the closer to bedtime, the more sleep people lost.
In five studies, people did not report more time awake in the night.

item.statement: In studies, caffeine added time awake in the night. Yet in five of them, people did not report being awake more.
item.why: Across 24 studies, caffeine made falling asleep slower and time awake longer; in five, people did not report more time awake.

lines.short: After caffeine, people slept about 45 minutes less than on nights without caffeine.
lines.but: The people studied were healthy adults with low to moderate usual caffeine intake, so heavy users, teenagers and older adults may differ.
how: 24 studies compared nights after caffeine with nights without it, in the same people.
Caffeine made falling asleep slower, time awake in the night longer, and sleep lighter.
The more caffeine, and the closer to bedtime, the more sleep people lost.
In five studies, people did not report more time awake in the night.

item.statement: Most volunteers in one lab study ranked a single session on psilocybin, the magic-mushroom drug, among their 5 most meaningful experiences.
item.why: Two months later, 67 in 100 did. But everyone in that study already took part in religious or spiritual activities, which may have made them see it as more spiritual.

lines.short: It can: most people in one lab study scored as having a full mystical experience. Two months later, 67 in 100 ranked it among their 5 most meaningful experiences.
lines.but: Everyone in that study already took part in religious or spiritual activities, which may have made them see it as more spiritual.
how: At Johns Hopkins, 36 healthy people new to psychedelics took part. 30 got psilocybin once and a stimulant once, 2 months apart, in random order.

Mystical here means high questionnaire scores for things like unity and sacredness: 19 of 30 had a full mystical experience on psilocybin. A trial in people with drinking problems also found high scores.

Two months on, 19 of the 24 who answered said it had raised their wellbeing, against 5 after the stimulant. People close to them saw a small change for the better; personality and mood tests showed no difference.
On psilocybin, 11 of 36 felt strong or extreme fear at some point, and 3 said they'd never want to repeat it.

item.statement: In lab studies, about 1 in 11 volunteers reported a short flashback after LSD or psilocybin, the drug in magic mushrooms.
item.why: Of 142 healthy lab volunteers, 13 said they had a flashback, usually a few seconds of changed seeing.

lines.short: About 1 in 11 lab volunteers reported a short flashback, mostly in the days after.
lines.but: These were healthy, screened volunteers in labs, with no drug-free group to compare.
how: 142 healthy adults took LSD, psilocybin or both in lab studies in Switzerland.
At the end, 13 said they had had a flashback, usually a few seconds of changed seeing.
Most did not mind it; 2 people were upset by it.
Nobody was found to have the long-lasting vision condition doctors call HPPD.

item.statement: Scans show serotonin changes in people who used ecstasy, and these changes are known to be permanent.
item.why: Nobody knows: three studies found more of the scan marker in people who had stopped longer ago, two found no link with time, and no one has been scanned while using and again years later.

lines.short: We do not know if the marker goes back to normal after people stop.
lines.but: Nobody has been scanned while using and then again years later.
how: Three studies compared different people and found more marker in those who stopped longer ago.
Two other studies found no link with time since the last pill.
People who stop may be different from people who keep going.
The parts that looked normal again are not where the drop is biggest.

item.statement: Cannabis is linked to car crashes just as strongly once studies take drivers' drinking into account.
item.why: It shrinks: studies that allowed for alcohol found about 1.1 to 1.2 times the odds of a crash, against 1.7 to 1.8 in studies that didn't. These compare crashed drivers with others, so they can't show one driver's chance of crashing.

lines.short: Drivers with cannabis in a test were linked to more crashes.
lines.but: These studies compare crashed drivers with others, so they cannot show one driver's chance of crashing.
how: Across 28 results from 21 studies in 13 countries, drivers with cannabis found in a test had about 1.2 to 1.4 times the odds of a crash, or of being at fault in one.
An older review found 1.9 times. Re-checking its counts and allowing for other factors brought the same studies to between 1.2 and 1.4.
Studies that allowed for alcohol found 1.1 to 1.2 times. Studies that did not found 1.7 to 1.8 times.
A positive test shows cannabis was in the body, not that a driver was impaired.
